Root: Why did the reported trial-to-paid conversion rate fall last month versus the prior comparable cohort?
Assumption: conversion means paid accounts divided by eligible trials, measured over equal maturation windows. Confirm this before attributing causes.

Diagnostic tree:
├─ Apparent decline: measurement/cohort comparability changed
│  ├─ Tracking or numerator/denominator definition changed — hypothesis; evidence absent; analytics owner TBD.
│  └─ Trials have not had equal time to convert — hypothesis; evidence absent; analytics owner TBD.
└─ Real decline under comparable measurement
   ├─ Trial mix changed: lower-converting sources/segments gained share — hypothesis; growth owner TBD.
   └─ Within comparable segments, conversion fell
      ├─ Fewer reached purchase decision — activation/use barriers; product owner TBD.
      └─ More reached it but declined — value/price/trust/procurement; commercial owner TBD.

Decomposition: measurement validity, then mix versus within-segment change, then funnel stage. Interactions and unknown segments mean completeness is provisional; assign each loss to one funnel stage to avoid overlap.

First analysis: analytics owner should verify cohort maturity, definitions, and instrumentation, then obtain segment volumes and conversion. Prioritize the branch explaining the largest observed change; no causal branch is established yet.

Inversion premortem: imagine Friday's migration corrupts or loses customer data. These are failure hypotheses, not forecasts; restoration and rollback being untested are user-provided facts.

| Failure condition | Mechanism | Severity / plausibility | Early signal | Safeguard / proposed owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Backup cannot restore | Failure leaves no recovery path | Critical / unknown | Restore fails validation | Restore to isolated environment before go/no-go; database lead |
| Rollback fails or takes too long | Partial migration strands writes | Critical / unknown | Rehearsal exceeds recovery window | Timed rollback including writes and reconciliation; migration lead |
| Records silently change or disappear | Mapping/constraints mishandle data | Critical / unknown | Count/checksum/business-rule mismatch | Representative rehearsal and reconciliation; data owner |

Top safeguards: demonstrate recoverability, demonstrate rollback, validate data integrity. Assign named people to proposed roles before proceeding.

Stop condition: do not authorize Friday's production migration without successful rehearsals against agreed recovery-time and data-loss limits. Review evidence at Thursday's go/no-go; if insufficient time remains, defer.

Residual risk includes production-only edge cases; use a bounded first batch and monitoring. Keep rehearsals targeted so controls do not prevent the migration indefinitely.

Eisenhower Matrix fits because urgency and importance determine this week's order.

| Quadrant | Task | Reason | Action | Proposed owner | Due/review |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Important and urgent | Customer outage | Active customer harm | Contain and restore service promptly | Incident lead | Now; review after restoration |
| Important, not urgent | Strategy due next month | Material future work; deadline not immediate | Protect two feasible work blocks this week | Strategy owner | Book today; review Friday |
| Neither, provisionally | Optional meeting tomorrow | Optionality alone supplies no material goal or cost of delay | Decline or request an asynchronous update | Invitee | Before tomorrow |

Assumptions: strategy is consequential; the optional meeting has no hidden decision or obligation. Reclassify the meeting if missing it causes a material delay. A calendar date alone does not make attendance urgent.

Capacity: outage response takes precedence; schedule strategy only within remaining capacity and communicate displaced commitments. No delegation without an owner accepting the handoff.

Prevention to investigate: whether this outage class recurs and which preventive action could reduce future urgent work. Review priorities after service restoration.

Connection Circles fits the requested causal map. Boundary: support queue over the coming days/weeks; every mechanism below is a hypothesis with unverified confidence.

Variables arranged around the circle: unresolved backlog B, waiting time W, follow-up message rate F, capacity spent on follow-ups C, capacity available for resolution R.

| Link | Hypothesized mechanism | Delay / evidence |
|---|---|---|
| B +→ W | More queued work delays service | Queue-dependent; unverified |
| W +→ F | Waiting customers ask for updates | Customer-dependent; unverified |
| F +→ C | Follow-ups consume handling time | Immediate/short; unverified |
| C −→ R | Fixed staff time leaves less resolution capacity | Short; unverified |
| R −→ B | More resolution capacity clears more tickets | Queue-dependent; unverified |

Closed loop: B→W→F→C→R→B has two negative links, so it is reinforcing: growth in backlog can amplify itself. It can also unwind if capacity frees up; this is not a quantitative forecast.

Leverage hypothesis: proactive updates reduce follow-ups; unintended effect could be more notification-driven replies. Test on a bounded queue. Measure arrivals, resolutions, follow-up handling time, and staffing; these missing drivers could explain backlog independently. Review after a comparable measurement period.

After Action Review fits one completed launch and includes both favorable and unfavorable gaps.

| Step | Finding | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Intended | Ship on the planned date with expected support volume | Reconstructed from your wording; retrieve original targets |
| Actual | Launch was late; tickets were below expectation | User-provided claims; confirm timestamps and counts |
| Gap | Worse timeliness; fewer tickets, whose meaning is unresolved | No sales/exposure denominator supplied |
| Why | Delay cause unknown. Low tickets could reflect quality, lower sales, or reporting/access differences | Competing hypotheses, not findings |
| Sustain | Provisionally retain the current launch support monitoring while testing whether it detects problems | Hypothesis; low volume does not prove success |
| Improve | Review schedule deviations against the launch timeline; normalize support by customers/exposure | Required before causal lessons |

Lessons: track service outcomes per exposed customer; preserve original targets; change launch practices only when competing explanations have been checked.

Next action: proposed launch owner assembles planned/actual milestones, sales or active-user exposure, ticket categories, and team/customer perspectives. Review when those data are available, before the next launch plan is finalized. Repeat a quality practice only if evidence identifies it; do not credit the delay with better quality yet.

Concept Map fits semantic relationships rather than causal behavior.

Focus question: How do revenue, gross margin, fixed costs, and profit relate in a simple business income statement?

Concept inventory:
- Revenue: recognized sales before costs.
- Cost of goods sold (COGS): costs assigned to goods/services sold.
- Gross profit: revenue minus COGS.
- Gross margin: gross profit divided by revenue; undefined when revenue is zero.
- Fixed operating costs: operating costs relatively unchanged over a stated activity range/time horizon.
- Profit: specify the level; below means operating profit.

Hierarchy: financial performance → revenue and expenses → gross profit → operating profit; gross margin is a ratio describing gross profit relative to revenue.

Propositions, high confidence under this simplified scope:
Revenue —minus COGS yields→ gross profit.
Gross profit —divided by revenue yields→ gross margin.
Gross profit —minus operating expenses yields→ operating profit.
Operating expenses —include→ fixed operating costs.

Cross-link: fixed versus variable classifies cost behavior; it does not equal COGS versus operating expenses. Some COGS may be fixed.

Gap: confirm whether your company uses “gross margin” for the ratio or monetary gross profit, and whether “profit” means operating or net profit. Net profit also reflects non-operating items and tax.

Verdict: 1 critical error. The causal conclusion is not established.

Argument structure: premise—signups increased after the redesign; thesis—the redesign caused that increase; inference—inductive causal attribution from temporal sequence.

| Location | Error | Why it fails | Repair needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| “Therefore … caused” | False cause — post hoc ergo propter hoc | Earlier timing alone cannot distinguish redesign effects from traffic changes, marketing, seasonality, or measurement changes | Compare credible controls and examine competing explanations |

Hidden premise: nothing else that could explain the increase changed, and signups were measured comparably. Neither is supplied.

Formal validity versus material truth: this is an inductive inference, so deductive validity is not the appropriate standard. The reported timing and increase are unverified user-provided premises; the redesign's causal effect remains unknown, not disproved.

Inductive strength: weak from the evidence given. A randomized comparison or credible comparison group, stable measurement, and checks for concurrent changes could strengthen or weaken the attribution. Identity and consistency show no visible defect; sufficient support for the causal claim is missing.

Verdict: 2 errors—1 critical overgeneralization and 1 contestable unstated assumption.

Argument structure: two beta users loved the feature; therefore every customer will buy it. This generalizes from a small sample and infers purchase from liking.

| Location | Error | Why it fails | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| “every customer” | Hasty generalization | Two potentially unrepresentative users cannot establish universal demand | Limit the claim to early interest |
| “will buy” | Unsupported inference | Liking does not establish willingness or ability to pay | Mark purchase demand as untested |

Hidden premises: beta users represent every customer; liking entails buying. Both are unsupported. The taxonomy supplies no Latin name for these defects.

Formal validity versus material truth: this is weak induction, not a deductive proof. The two positive reactions are user-provided and unverified; universal purchasing remains unsupported. No explicit contradiction or change in word meaning is evident.

Rewrite: “Two beta users loved the feature—an encouraging start. Whether customers will buy it is still untested.”

Changelog: removed universal prediction; preserved the concise positive tone; separated observed enthusiasm from buying behavior.

Verdict: invalid—1 critical error, affirming the consequent.

Structure: premises P→Q and Q; conclusion P. No hidden premise is needed to expose the invalidity. Adding Q→P would repair it, but that premise is absent.

Counterexample row:

| P | Q | P→Q | Q premise | P conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| False | True | True | True | False |

Both premises can be true while the conclusion is false, so the form fails the truth-preservation test.

Concrete example: “If it rains, the pavement is wet. The pavement is wet. Therefore it rained.” A sprinkler can wet the pavement without rain.

The error is affirming the consequent; the provided taxonomy gives no Latin alias. Q may hold for a reason other than P. Identity and non-contradiction are not the issue.

Formal validity and truth are separate: this form is invalid regardless of whether P and Q happen to be true in a particular instance. The abstract task supplies no factual truth values; the counterexample assigns possible values rather than claiming actual facts.

Six Thinking Hats compares perspectives; Inversion tests the provisional choice.

Focus: launch now or run a small pilot?
White: demand unknown; broad launch expensive to reverse; pilot cheap—all supplied by you.
Red: stakeholder intuitions have not been supplied.
Yellow: launch may capture demand sooner; pilot may buy learning cheaply. Both benefits are hypotheses.
Black: launch risks costly commitment without demand; pilot risks misleading samples and delay.
Green: pilot with representative users, an actual buying decision, spending cap, and expansion gate.
Blue: provisionally choose the pilot. Proposed owner: product lead. Set success, failure, and stop thresholds before starting; review at its agreed end.

Hand-off to Inversion: this bounded pilot is the plan to challenge.

| Failure hypothesis | Mechanism / severity / plausibility | Signal | Safeguard / owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Enthusiasts misrepresent buyers | False demand confidence / high / unknown | Interest without payment | Include target buyers and test paid commitment / product lead |
| Delay destroys opportunity | Learning arrives too late / high / unknown | Credible deadline or competitor lock-in | Bound duration and assess delay cost / commercial lead |

Stop if exposure or spend breaches limits. Residual risk: a pilot may not predict scale. Reconsider launch-now only with credible urgency and bounded downside.

I cannot rank the vendors without inventing options, preferences, and evidence. Before building the Decision Matrix:

1. Which three vendors, what are you buying, who owns the decision, and when must it be made? Is keeping the current solution a viable baseline?
2. What are the non-negotiable constraints—such as budget, required capabilities, data handling, or implementation deadline—and which decision criteria matter most?
3. What comparable evidence do you have for each vendor: full cost, capabilities, reliability, implementation effort, contractual risks, and unresolved questions?

Once supplied, we can screen hard constraints, define non-overlapping criteria and anchored scores, agree weights before scoring, and mark missing evidence explicitly. Then we will check whether plausible changes in uncertain scores or weights reverse the ranking.

Provisional matrix: vendor columns A/B/C plus baseline; criteria, weights, scores, and totals remain unfilled. No preferred vendor is supportable yet. The choice should be revisited if pricing, constraints, or key evidence changes.
